title: Your own body
hook: several traditions honor the body as gift or temple

segments.voice: Yesterday, the difficult people. Your line was the hard ones too. Did a quiet wish go to someone hard? Today, a closer neighbor than any of them: the one you live inside. Day eight hundred fifty-nine.

Knees that click on the stairs. A back that votes against getting out of bed. A face under the bathroom light at seven in the morning. For some people, the harshest words of the whole day are never said out loud. They're said silently, to their own body. Meanwhile that same body has been breathing all night without being asked, healing a paper cut nobody thanked it for, and carrying its owner to the bathroom mirror to be criticized. This block of the path is about love. Today it turns to the one thing anyone hearing this is living in.
screen: `KNEES THAT CLICK ON THE STAIRS.` → `WORDS SAID SILENTLY TO A BODY.` → `BREATHING ALL NIGHT, UNTHANKED.`

segments.voice: First, fearfully and wonderfully made. In the Psalms, a singer looks at their own body and starts praising: "I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made." Not perfectly made. Not admired by others. Wonderfully made, with a little awe mixed in. In that psalm, the body is a gift and a wonder before it's anything else. Second, a temple, not a project. Writing to Christians in Corinth who were arguing about what they could do with their bodies, Paul asks: "know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you". In context, Paul is warning them about how they use their bodies, and the image he picks raises the stakes: a temple is holy, a place where God dwells, not something to use carelessly. Third, the Buddha accepts a meal. In a sutta in the Middle Length Discourses, the Buddha remembers his life before awakening. He tried to wring freedom out of his body by starving it, until it was skin and bone. It didn't work. Then he remembered sitting peacefully under a tree as a boy, and he asked whether that kind of ease was really something to fear. He decided it wasn't, and he took solid food again. In the story, the way forward began with a meal. Fourth, kind, not perfect. None of these texts asks for a body that looks a certain way. They ask for something smaller: reverence, care, an end to treating it as an enemy. Sleep when it's tired. Feed it. Stop the silent insults for one day. This body, as it is.
screen: `FEARFULLY AND WONDERFULLY MADE.` · `A TEMPLE, NOT A PROJECT.` · `THE BUDDHA ACCEPTS A MEAL.` · `KIND, NOT PERFECT.` · then, large: `THIS BODY.`

segments.voice: Sit or lie down, whatever is kind to your back right now. Start at the feet. Feel them, and silently thank them for today's steps. Move up slowly: legs, belly, hands, shoulders, the face. Wherever there's an ache, don't argue with it; just rest your attention there for a breath, the way you'd sit with a friend who's tired. If the old critical words show up, let them pass and go back to thanks. If you pray, you can give thanks to God for this body. The bell holds the time.
Temple. Paul's word for the body: a place where God dwells, to be cared for, not used carelessly. Today's word.
Your line: this body. Today, do one kind thing for it on purpose: a glass of water, a real lunch, a walk, an earlier night. And catch one silent insult before it lands. Day eight hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Some Christians speak of the body as a temple, after Paul's letter to the Corinthians; Jews and Christians pray the Psalms, including the praise of being wonderfully made; Buddhists tell how the Buddha left behind extreme fasting and took food before his awakening.

original.note: the Greek word for temple that Paul uses in 1 Corinthians 6:19.

trapdoor: what you thought: loving your body means liking how it looks.
what it means: it means treating it as a gift and a temple: cared for, fed, rested.
what a scholar hears: in the Middle Length Discourses, the Buddha's path turns when he gives up self-starvation and eats, so care for the body sits inside the story of awakening.

notes: Audit pass: 1 Corinthians 6 is about sexual conduct, not self-punishment; replaced the narrator's gloss 'a temple is cared for, not punished' (teach and match pair) with what the image says in context (holy, God's dwelling, not to be used carelessly).
The outline hook says 'most traditions honor the body'; the script and hook field soften this to 'several traditions' under the claims rule.

MN 36 retelling is paraphrased: the austerities, the memory of a peaceful childhood moment under a tree, the reflection that this ease need not be feared, and taking solid food. The Sujata milk-rice story is later tradition and is deliberately left out.

Editor pass: cut the unsourced claim 'Christians have read that line in a lot of directions, about food, about sex, about rest', replacing it with what the context of 1 Corinthians 6 says (how they use their bodies); fixed the hook's 'every reader of this sentence' (an audio lesson has listeners, not readers).
ναός: confirm the form and the stress mark; the pronunciation given is an approximation.
The psalm's singer is left unnamed ('a singer'); the psalm's heading attributes it to David, which the script does not state.
